story_text.value:
anthropic pads claude's text because it wants you to read slower. claude-isms and the amount of text in a claude-code session are tailored so that you spend more time processing a large prompt. It's much easier to write 150k words once than 10k words twice.

If you can increase the quality of outputs, we can spend more time reading. But, people typically don't read the dot-mark-down-md.

what if there was a double-wide claude-code that automatically showed each file it touched in a collapsible list

accessible with vim keybinds, of course.

story_text.value:
I look up a lot at the sky at night and made this because I wanted to better understand what is up there.

Orbital shows all 32,000+ tracked objects at their current positions: about 17,000 working satellites, 2,800 dead ones, 2,200 spent rocket bodies and 10,700 pieces of debris.

Each is color coded, can be switched off, and can be "clicked" to follow. For the well-known ones it pulls up a real photo (where available), what it is for, and when it stopped working.

There is an animation that shows launch history from 1957 to today. When you first visit, click on the "Watch 1957 → today" button to see the animation.

You can also "fly out" to the solar system and see the planets, moons, comets and spacecraft further out there.

My orbit data comes from Space-Track. I also pull from CelesTrak to determine which satellites are currently active.

It is a static site on GitHub Pages (currently) with no backend, no accounts, and no ads. It also installs as an app and reopens offline.

I wrote it with Claude Code doing most of the implementation. I will provide the link to the source if you want it.

I would like to hear what you think about it. Specifically, what is confusing on a first visit, and what would make you come back to it. And anything else constructive you would like to share.

title.value: Show HN: Orbital – Everything (known) in Earth orbit, live in 3D, in the browser

story_text.value:
This open-source TUI and CLI allows running the workflows that android devs run every day without leaving the terminal and each one in their own worktree.

You can see the agents working in a control pane with different status. The TUI will inform you when it needs your help.

You can: 1. Create a Pull Request from a ticket, the harness does a plan -> code -> review workflow. You can decide the model per state. 2. Auto fix the ticket comments, the harness fetches the PR comments and show it in the dashboard. You can previsualize and approve or request a new fix. 3. Review the diff, the TUI has a beauty diff viewer so you can review the code without leaving the terminal. 4. Open the worktree in Android Studio or claude code directly from the TUI. 5. Permission and budget management: you can auto approve comments or approve once. You can also set a spend limit per stage.

It is optimized for android: 1. Only one agent at a time can take control of the emulator. 2. The worktree creation, all git operations and PR information is deterministic and handled by the harness taking into consideration how Android projects are built. 3. Open the worktree in Android Studio. 4. Open the emulator from the TUI.

Caveats: For now it only works for Claude Code.

story_text.value:
Hey HN, I'm Daniel, founder of Onlook (https://github.com/onlook-dev/onlook and onlook.com).

Onlook is a desktop app that puts a canvas on top of your real codebase, letting you design directly in code with the agent you already use. Over 25,000 designers and developers have supported the project, 100+ have contributed, and it's been the #1 trending repo in the world twice. We just rebuilt the entire product as an agentic design tool, and open-sourced it to the community.

Here’s a demo video: (https://youtu.be/BogcYWf4siM)

If you're an engineer, traditional engineering tools are largely built for convergence, whereas designers tend to explore and diverge on ideas. Onlook gives designers a familiar canvas while managing all of the dev processes that get between them and making mind-blowing designs in code. Designers can work on a multiple simultaneous worktrees that run on the real app locally, and every change lands as a PR you can review or throw away, so there aren’t mockups to rebuild.

We built Onlook because we believe there needs to be a developer tool that works the way designers do.

More and more, designers are expected to work in code. Designers think by seeing, drafting, arranging variations, using references, and remixing ideas. That’s why the canvas has been the signature feature of design tools because it genuinely is useful for how messy the creative process is. Most of the challenge of using engineering tools for design work is that the first half of starting a project often takes mental bandwidth in of itself (What branch am I on? What page was that last exploration on?) and the second half is constrained by configuring your coded design to present itself (prompting design tools on top of what you’ve built or making temporary navigation for that specific state).

Some of you may remember our earlier Show HNs (July 2024: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=40904862, August 2024: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=41390449, May 2025: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=44127653). Since then, we built a web version (too early), then a Storybook-native build (a mistake). We noticed that our desktop product from July 2024 was still getting hundreds of downloads a month despite zero promotion, so we decided to rebuild it for the new era of designers working in code.

How it works…

Onlook shines at exploring tons of ideas at once. Ask it to lay out every flow in your product, show every state of a component, or riff on ten versions of one screen. Your designs all show up side by side on an infinite canvas, with each frame as a real webview running your actual app with real data. Not as a mockup, but the real deal.

When we built this editor, we had an epiphany that it could be a new kind of IDE for design. Design tools used to be limited to a proprietary setup or closed schema, but now you can push and pull the medium of code to get whatever result you want, so why not give agents an infinite canvas of browsers and see what they do? It turns out, the agents can figure out how to better present coded work by adjusting the urls of browser frames and arranging and resizing them on the canvas.

The concept is simple, but it requires a lot of product thinking. For example, because all of the frames on the canvas share a single browser session, and Chromium only allows six connections per host per session, ten frames of the same app end up fighting over limited connections. So, we had to plan around that, and there are still tons of things we need to do to make the canvas ultra performant.

Onlook is an Electron app where you can import a repo from GitHub or upload a local folder. Then, Onlook creates a git worktree, starts your dev server, and has the agent sort out missing dependencies or other requirements. You never open a terminal and everything the agent does is a normal git diff that can go to GitHub as a PR. We inject a small script into each frame that draws selection outlines and reads the page, so that way you can click an element, say "make this a card layout," and the agent knows exactly what "this" is.

This time we didn't build our own agent. Onlook runs Claude Code or Codex on your own subscription, and we turn whatever the agent emits into one typed event log and draw the UI from that in our own chat interface. On top of that we give the agent a bespoke set of design-specific tools, from arranging frames on the canvas, to making suggestions, to generating multiple iterations of a selection – which is especially useful because the agent decides how to get the app into a state that you need based on your prompt.

We also have our own Artifacts which are quick HTML sketches that live in the editor, but outside your repo. They’re almost like components in other design tools in that they can be carried and edited across every project but are detached from the project with no network access. As an example, you can ask the agent to turn your interface into an Artifact, and use it as a reference for another exploration, or download it as HTML and send it to a coworker as an interactive export of something you have in progress. I frequently go back to the artifacts I’ve made as visual snippets when I need new ideas or need to borrow something that’s already been built.

The desktop editor is free (you can download it from our website at onlook.com) and open source under Apache-2.0, and we'll eventually offer a paid cloud product for teams.

We'd love to hear which repos work and which don't, what you try to do on the canvas, and what's missing. We’re so excited for this to be a new way for designers to work in code!

The Onlook team (Joel - thebrubaker and Kris - krisodd), and I will be here all day!

title.value: Launch HN: Onlook (YC W25) – An open-source developer tool for designers

story_text.value:
Founder here, I posted the beta version of ToolJet on HN in 2021 as a no-code/low-code builder. Ended up getting 400 upvotes.

I wrote the first version in 7 weeks during the covid lockdown, and the drag and drop builder was the whole product. Over the last few months our customers wanted the UI flexibility and convenience of vibe coding without giving up the governance they came to ToolJet for. We resisted for a while.

We did not pivot, but we did rebuild the app builder so an app can be built with code or without it. The frontend of apps is a React codebase, written by Claude Code, Codex, Cursor or by hand, and ToolJet is the platform it runs on.

How it works: - Internal tools can be generated using your own coding agents or using our agent.

- Frontend is React codebase, it can be edited from our app builder, VS code, or any other IDE.Code will be scanned for security issues before saving. Scanning policies can be set by admins.

- Frontend never interacts with APIs, databases or other data sources. Every interaction with data source goes through our backend where we enforce access control. We have 100+ data source integrations.

- Platform comes with version, environment and release management.

- Changes can be reviewed visually as well before promoting to prod. Workflows can be setup to have reviewers and reviews/approvals.

- Platform handles SSO, RBAC and more granular access control.

Would love to hear where this breaks for you.

title.value: Show HN: ToolJet 4.0 – vibe-code internal tools with governance

story_text.value:
Hi. I made small project called Zpup. It takes small 3D scene written in JSON and gives back a flat SVG from any angle. There is no JavaScript in the file, so it works in img-tag or README.

I needed 3D for small project at my company, and Zdog make big impression on me. But Zdog has not had a release for several years, so I wanted to make modern version.

One thing works different. Zdog sorts each shape by one point. so small thing on big floor gets covered when you turn it. Zpup compares the shapes that overlap. You can see both in the README.

I wrote it with Claude Code Fable 5.2.

No canvas renderer, no text shape, and it is 0.2 version.

Playground: https://rxolve.github.io/zpup

Feedback is always welcome :)

story_text.value:
I have started using multiple models (Claude, Codex, Grok via cursor-agent, Z.ai, Deepseek, Hy4 via OpenCode, agy) etc, and I realized that I not able to identify which commit was made by which model. After looking around and not finding anything, I create a format specification that will let Model self-identify itself. The goal is a higher ranked model can verify the output of other models and suggest changes. It is similar how to a Senior Engineer will review the output of Junior Engineers. As Humans, we know which model is behaving well, and which we can trust more.

My AI based commits have a identification like this.

Add retry backoff to fetch

Model: claude-sonnet-5-5 harness=claude-code effort=high conf=medium

Model: opencode/hy4-flash-free harness=opencode effort=high conf=medium

In using this, I get an intuition what I can expect when I fire off model on a particular task.

title.value: Show HN: Git Hook for Model Identifation

As a Ubuntu user, it was just brought to my attention that /tmp is now mounted on tmpfs (aka your RAM).

Coding agents, like Claude Code, use /tmp as a scratchpad for files, model weights, etc.

Therefore, if you have RAM constraints, consider setting CLAUDE_CODE_TMPDIR to e.g. ~/.claude/tmp

story_text.value:
Hey, I'm Matt. This is a free game I built in the spirit of the old internet. Just built for fun and no other reason. I built a version 2-3 years ago by hand. This time I built it assisted by Claude Code.

Every day you set a toggle. On/off, dials, etc. Every single one of them follows some piece of public data.

The board locks at 23:00 UTC and is scored. You then find out what was right or wrong. On some toggles there's also an indicator if you are hot or cold. The goal is to get them all right :).

Hints are given along at checkpoints along the way.

I have an open beta beginning November 30th. Would love to get feedback on the concept, what works, what doesn't, etc so that season 1 goes off without too many hitches.

story_text.value:
Hey HN, I’m Tony. I’m a co-founder of Springcraft, where we have been doing a lot of CAD modeling for robot parts. Our team kept running into limitations with existing kernels, and so I decided to write a new B-rep kernel and a new comprehensive, kernel-agnostic B-rep conformance test suite. Both are available today under MIT licenses.

The kernel, springrep, is written in safe Rust with no dependencies. It covers a broad range of our mechanical CAD needs, including advanced fillets, sweeps, lofts, shells, offsets, STEP and exact measurements and queries. Claude Code made it feasible to write this, but it took a lot of time and care to get it right.

The test suite, brep-conformance, has 3,487 cases covering the modeling operations common across kernels: booleans, fillets, chamfers, shells, offsets, sweeps, lofts, STEP, and queries with expected answers coming from closed forms and exact geometry. It caught hundreds of bugs, edge cases, and hot spots in springrep that our own tests had missed, and now springrep passes all of it. We’ve also run it on a few popular open-source kernels and anyone can run it on theirs. This is the first version, so there are surely mistakes in the test and adapters. Corrections, pull requests, and new kernels are welcome.

kernel: https://github.com/springcraft-ai/springrep conformance suite: https://springcraft-ai.github.io/brep-conformance/

story_text.value:
As a solo-dev with a lot of projects going on, I found myself needing to make short promos or explainer videos. Not being familiar with animation software, I had the idea to use Claude to code up those videos and export them as video files. Note that this was before AI-coded music videos went viral, back in the early days when the models were just getting good enough to make the result actually look good.

In the process of creating these clips I stumbled into a bunch of bugs and setup needed to make it work reliably. The list of features I wanted for better control and feedback kept growing and I needed to sign up for a bunch of services to get music, voiceovers and other media into my project. I couldn't find an existing service that had everything I wanted. Seeing these hurdles and that the technology was only easily accessible to people already confident with coding agents, I started working on Klistra, and a couple of months later I'm turning it into a service so you all can use it too.

The goal with Klistra was to include everything I missed in the manual workflow into an easy to use service with a nice UI, so people could focus on what they wanted the video to look like, not setting up the framework behind it. Klistra includes precise timeline control, media generation, built in support to make animations match the rhythm of the background music, word extraction from voiceovers or songs, a dedicated iteration / feedback tool, web scraper and much more.

Something I knew I needed to get right was making it easy to iterate on small features of the video with precise control of what was being built. I designed Klistra so you first create a specification where you define scenes in detail, describe what you want shown and when, reference media or timestamps in-line, freely drag the timeline around and preview the result before letting a builder agent create the video. If you want to change something, the specification changes and the builder agent gets a diff of what changed. This way there is always a written specification that matches the render / build. There is also a planner agent built into Klistra that helps create and edit the specification for you (which is what I use the most), while letting you turn to manual fine-tuning when needed.

Don't think of this as a replacement for diffusion models, if you want photorealistic images or videos they clearly do a better job. Klistra really shines when you need motion design and precise control, exact text with your fonts, media such as logos or voiceovers, animated UI that matches your apps and so on. Klistra does have built in integrations for generating media from diffusion models, and combining the two technologies usually gets the best results.

Everything that costs money to run on Klistra, from machines to AI tokens, is paid for with credits included in a subscription or bought via one time packs (Pro starting at $25/mo and packs at $12). Being a solo-dev without funding, the budget wouldn't allow for a free tier with enough monthly credits for a real project. I instead decided to give the first 200 of you who sign up 350 free credits, enough for a simple video (the advanced tutorial used around 250 credits).

I created tutorials covering the basics. Mostly relying on the planner: https://klistra.ai/docs/basic and for advanced features and manual control: https://klistra.ai/docs/advanced

You can see demo videos on the home page https://klistra.ai/ and on the tutorial pages. I would love to see what you make!

Some additional notes:

- After feedback from friends there is also a Claude Code integration in paid subscriptions, where your agent can act as a planner, convenient if you already have a project built with Claude that has all the context and you need an explainer, ad or social post. It also reduces credit spending if you're a heavy planner user.

- Klistra can create images too.

Happy to hear what you think!
